value: Recent failures in neuropathic pain clinical trials have prompted speculation that increasing placebo responses may diminish drug-placebo separation. To investigate this, data from published randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of neuropathic pain drugs conducted between 1990 and 2013 were analyzed. Findings revealed a considerable increase in placebo responses over this period, while drug responses remained stable, resulting in a diminished treatment advantage. This trend was primarily driven by trials conducted in the United States, where increases in study size and length, factors associated with larger placebo responses, were also observed. Furthermore, analysis of individual RCT time courses showed that treatment responses evolved more quickly and plateaued within four weeks, unlike placebo responses. This highlights a significant and growing challenge for demonstrating efficacy in neuropathic pain drug development, particularly in US-based trials.
